{{short description|Soviet mathematician}}
{{distinguish|Sergey Vladimirovich Fomin}}
'''Sergei Vasilyevich Fomin''' ({{langx|ru|Серге́й Васи́льевич Фоми́н}}; 9 December 1917 &ndash; 17 August 1975) was a  [[USSR|Soviet]] [[mathematician]] who was co-author with [[Andrey Kolmogorov]] of ''Introductory real analysis'',<ref>{{cite book|last1=Kolmogorov|first1=Andrey Nikolaevich|author1-link=Andrey Kolmogorov|last2=Fomin|first2=Sergei Vasilyevich|title=Introductory real analysis|publisher=Dover Publications|location=New York|orig-year=1970|date=1975|isbn=978-0-486-61226-3|url-access=registration|url=https://archive.org/details/introductoryreal00kolm_0}}.</ref> and co-author with [[Israel Gelfand]] of ''Calculus of Variations'' (1963),<ref>{{cite book|last1=Gelfand|first1=Israel Moisevich|author1-link=Israel Gelfand|last2=Fomin|first2=Sergei Vasilyevich|title=Calculus of variations|publisher=Dover Publications|location=Mineola, New York|orig-year=1963|date=2000|isbn=978-0-486-41448-5}}.</ref> both books that are widely read in Russian and in English.

Fomin entered [[Moscow State University]] at the age of 16. His first paper was published at 19 on infinite [[abelian group]]s. After his graduation he worked with Kolmogorov. He was drafted during [[World War II]], after which he returned to Moscow.

When the war ended Fomin returned to Moscow State University and joined [[Andrey Nikolayevich Tikhonov|Andrey Tikhonov]]'s department. In 1951 he was awarded his habilitation for a dissertation on [[dynamical system]]s with invariant measure. Two years later he was appointed a professor. Later in life, he became involved with mathematical aspects of biology.

The American mathematician [[Paul Halmos]] wrote the following about Fomin:

''Some of the mathematical interests of Sergei Vasilovich were always close to some of mine (measure and ergodic theory); he supervised the translation of a couple of my books into Russian. We had corresponded before we met, and it was a pleasure to shake hands with a man instead of reading a letter. Three or four years later he came to visit me in Hawaii, and it was a pleasure to see him enjoy, in contrast to Moscow, the warm sunshine''.

Fomin died in [[Vladivostok]].
